planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall in gritty, well-drained, limestone-derived soil in part shade; this Illyrian-Adriatic species is named for its finely cut, almost thread-like leaf segments, a more delicate texture than the broader-leaved garden hybrids.

directions: Set divisions at the original soil depth in sharply drained, gritty, alkaline to neutral soil in part shade, choosing a site modeled on the species' native limestone hillsides of Italy, Slovenia, and the western Balkans. The deeply dissected, almost ferny foliage, cut into many narrow segments, distinguishes this species from the broader-leaved garden hybrids and gives it a fine, airy texture even when not in bloom. Nodding, saucer-shaped green flowers open in late winter and early spring above the clump. It resents heavy, waterlogged soil far more than most hellebores and performs best where winter wet drains away quickly from the crown.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to part shade; of all the hellebore species this small, slender plant is the most committed shade-lover, native to beech-wood clearings and streamside scrub from Croatia and Slovenia into Hungary.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full to part shade, sheltered from drying wind, recreating the beech-wood clearings and shaded streambanks of its native range across Croatia, Slovenia, and Hungary. This is a small, slender, deciduous species with finely divided green foliage that dies back in summer dormancy after an early spring flush of small, nodding, green flowers. It is markedly more shade-tolerant than most other species hellebores and is one of the earliest to emerge from the ground after winter, so avoid disturbing the crown in late winter when new growth is pushing up.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in part shade to full sun; this recently distinguished northern Croatian species, closely related to H. torquatus and H. atrorubens, is a clump-forming deciduous perennial with purple-tinged, narrowly segmented leaves.

directions: Plant divisions in moisture-retentive but well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil, choosing a site in part shade or light sun that mirrors its native open woodland, hedgerows, and grazed floodplain terraces of northern Croatia. The rounded, deeply cut leaves often carry a purple flush, and in spring the clump sends up slightly nodding flowers of deep purple to reddish-purple with greenish interior tones, closely resembling its near relatives H. torquatus and H. atrorubens. It is an easygoing, undemanding species once established, tolerating more sun than most hellebores as long as the soil stays evenly moist through the growing season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall in well-drained, humus-rich, limestone-leaning soil in part shade; native to the margins of oak, ash, and beech woodland across the Balkans and northern Greece, this species takes its name from its rounded, circular leaf outline.

directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil with a neutral to alkaline pH, in part shade along a woodland edge or light scrub planting that recalls its native range from northern Greece through Albania and into the southern Balkans. The dark green, deeply palmate leaves spread in a distinctive circular outline, giving the species its name. In late winter and early spring, leafless flowering stalks rise above the foliage bearing open, green to yellow-green saucer-shaped flowers. It favors limestone-derived soils and benefits from a dry summer dormancy period similar to its native Mediterranean-influenced climate.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; this is the only hellebore native to Slovenia with dark flowers, found in open woods and upland pasture alongside wood anemone and snowdrops.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in part shade, in a setting similar to the open woods and upland pastures of Slovenia and Croatia where it grows alongside wood anemone, snowdrops, and lungwort. This deciduous species produces small flowers in late winter whose outer surface is deep purple and whose interior is mostly green, a dark, moody color combination unique among the Slovenian hellebore flora. It dies back to the rootstock in summer and resents being disturbed while dormant, so mark its location if planting nearby companions. Plants grown in the most exposed, sun-drenched parts of their range tend to develop the darkest flower color.
sources: Nature in Colour — Slovenian Flora Notes

common_name: Hugh Evans Camellia (Fragrant Single Pink Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade; Hugh Evans is a vigorous, arching sasanqua valued for its long fall-to-winter bloom season and light fragrance.

directions: Hugh Evans forms a vigorous, upright-and-spreading shrub with arching branches and neat, dark green foliage, well suited to a tall informal hedge or screen where a sasanqua with real size and presence is wanted. From late fall into winter it carries an unusually long, heavy succession of single, rose-pink flowers centered on a bold boss of gold stamens, with a light fragrance that is more noticeable than in most sasanquas. Grow in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, though established plants tolerate more sun if roots stay cool and evenly moist. Prune lightly right after the bloom season ends to control size, since flower buds for the following fall form on the current year's growth over summer.

common_name: Alabama Beauty Camellia (Rosy-Red Early Fall Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; Alabama Beauty, selected by a Semmes, Alabama nursery, is valued as one of the earliest sasanquas to open each fall and for tolerating more heat and sun than most.

directions: Alabama Beauty grows into a large, upright, vigorous shrub with dark, glossy, serrate-edged foliage, and is prized for opening its rosy-red to bright-pink, semi-double flowers earlier in fall than most sasanqua cultivars, giving an extended season of bloom when paired with later-flowering types. It tolerates heat and sun better than many camellias and can be grown in full sun once established, though it still performs best with part shade and consistent moisture. Its size and dense branching make it a strong choice for a tall flowering screen, mass hedge, or background planting. Grow in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring.

common_name: Lisa Camellia (Compact White Formal Double Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; Lisa is a compact, small-leaved sasanqua with symmetrical white rose-form to formal double flowers that open early in the fall season.

directions: Lisa is an upright, vigorous but compact sasanqua with small, neat leaves that give the whole plant a tidy, refined appearance even before it blooms. In early fall it produces white, rose-form to formal double flowers with an unusually symmetrical, tightly layered petal arrangement that holds its shape well over a long bloom period. Its moderate size and dense habit suit it to foundation plantings, narrow borders, or large containers where a tidy evergreen accent is wanted. Grow in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, and mulch to keep roots cool and evenly moist through summer heat.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; Shibori Egao ('smiling face') is a pink-and-white variegated sport of the classic sasanqua Egao and can be trained as a large shrub or small multi-stem tree.

directions: Shibori Egao bears semi-double to loose peony-form flowers splashed and streaked in pink over a white ground, giving each bloom a lively, hand-dyed appearance that gives the cultivar its name, meaning 'smiling face' in Japanese. It blooms in early to mid-fall on a large, vigorous shrub that can also be limbed up and trained into a small flowering tree where space allows. Grow in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, with some tolerance of fuller sun once the roots are established. Because it is a variegated sport, occasional reverted branches of solid pink may appear and should be pruned out to keep the patterned flower display consistent.
